title: 05 — Design Consistent Hashing
html:
05 — Design Consistent Hashing

The one idea: with hash(key) % n, changing n remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on the same ring so adding or removing a server moves only about 1/n of the keys — and virtual nodes keep the load even.

Step 1 — The rehashing problem

With 4 servers and server = hash(key) % 4, keys are spread evenly. Remove one server → % 3 → ~75% of keys map to a different server. For a cache that's a mass miss storm; for a data store it's a mass migration.

Goal: when a node joins or leaves, move as few keys as possible, and keep load even.

Step 2 — The hash ring

  1. Take a hash function with a large output space (e.g. the first 64 bits of SHA-1 / MurmurHash / xxHash).
  2. Bend the space into a ring: 0 → 2^64−1 → 0.
  3. Hash each server (by name/IP) onto the ring.
  4. Hash each key onto the ring; walk clockwise to the first server — that server owns the key.
---
title: Consistent hashing — the hash ring
---
flowchart LR
    s0["Server 0"] -- "ring, clockwise" --> k1(("key1")) --> s1["Server 1"]
    s1 -- "ring, clockwise" --> k2(("key2")) --> s2["Server 2"]
    s2 -- "ring, clockwise" --> k3(("key3")) --> s3["Server 3"]
    s3 -- "ring, clockwise" --> k0(("key0")) --> s0

Each key walks clockwise to the first server it meets: key1 → server 1, key2 → server 2, and so on; key0 wraps past the top of the ring to server 0.

  • Add server 4 between server 3 and server 0 → only the keys between server 3 and server 4 move (to server 4).
  • Remove server 1 → only server 1's keys move (to server 2).

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 Two problems with the basic ring

  1. Uneven partitions: with few servers placed randomly, one may own a huge arc.
  2. Uneven key distribution: even equal arcs can hold unequal keys.

3.2 Virtual nodes

Each physical server is placed on the ring many times (e.g. 100–200 virtual nodes: server0#0, server0#1, …). A key maps to a virtual node, which maps to its physical server.

More virtual nodes Effect
Load Standard deviation of load falls (≈ 5–10% at 100–200 vnodes)
Cost More memory for the ring's lookup table
Heterogeneous hardware Give bigger machines more vnodes

3.3 Finding affected keys

When server S is added: the affected range runs anticlockwise from S to the previous server; those keys move to S. When S is removed: the same range moves to the next server clockwise.

3.4 Lookup implementation

Keep a sorted array of vnode hashes → binary search for the first hash ≥ key hash (wrap to index 0). O(log V) per lookup.

public sealed class ConsistentHashRing<TNode>
{
    private readonly SortedDictionary<ulong, TNode> _ring = new();
    private ulong[] _keys = [];
    private readonly int _virtualNodes;

    public ConsistentHashRing(int virtualNodes = 150) => _virtualNodes = virtualNodes;

    public void Add(TNode node)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < _virtualNodes; i++)
            _ring[Hash($"{node}#{i}")] = node;
        _keys = [.. _ring.Keys];
    }

    public void Remove(TNode node)
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < _virtualNodes; i++)
            _ring.Remove(Hash($"{node}#{i}"));
        _keys = [.. _ring.Keys];
    }

    public TNode GetNode(string key)
    {
        ulong h = Hash(key);
        int idx = Array.BinarySearch(_keys, h);
        if (idx < 0) idx = ~idx;              // first element greater than h
        if (idx == _keys.Length) idx = 0;     // wrap around the ring
        return _ring[_keys[idx]];
    }

    private static ulong Hash(string s) =>
        System.IO.Hashing.XxHash64.HashToUInt64(System.Text.Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(s));
}

⚠️ Never use string.GetHashCode() for this — it is randomised per process in .NET Core, so two servers would disagree on the ring.

3.5 Alternatives worth naming

Scheme Idea Used by
Rendezvous (HRW) hashing For each key, score every node with hash(key, node); pick the max Simple, no ring; O(n) per lookup
Jump consistent hash Tiny, fast, perfectly even; nodes must be numbered 0..n−1 Good for sharded storage with append-only node lists
Maglev hashing Lookup table built for fast, even, minimally-disruptive LB Google's network load balancer
Fixed hash slots Pre-split into many slots (Redis Cluster: 16,384), assign slots to nodes Redis Cluster, Cosmos DB physical partitions

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Benefits: minimal key movement on scale events, horizontal scaling, and mitigation of hotspots (with vnodes).

Where it appears: Dynamo-style stores (DynamoDB partitioning, Cassandra token ring), Discord's chat routing, CDN and cache routing (Akamai), load balancers (Maglev).

Still unsolved by hashing alone: a single hot key (a celebrity) lands on one node however you hash — handle with caching, key splitting, or read replicas.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Azure Cache for Redis (clustered) — hash slots (CRC16(key) % 16384); use {hash tags} to force related keys onto one slot for multi-key ops.
  • Cosmos DB — logical partitions by partition key, hashed onto physical partitions; splits are handled for you.
  • Orleans — grain placement across silos uses a consistent-hash ring for its directory.
  • System.IO.Hashing (NuGet) gives XxHash64 / XxHash3 — stable across processes.

Review checklist

  • Explain why % n fails, with the "~all keys move" number.
  • Ring + clockwise lookup.
  • Virtual nodes and why (evenness, heterogeneous nodes).
  • Only neighbour range moves on add/remove.
  • Hot keys are a separate problem.
